maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil) (Superintendent General of Indian Affairs) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient,-
(1)	to confirm an agreement for the settlement of certain questions between the government of Canada and Ontario respecting Indian Reserve Lands, made the 24th March, 1924, defining the respective rights of each touching the disposition of lands in Indian Reserves in the Province which are surrendered by the Indians in order that they may be disposed for the benefit of the Band;
(2)	to authorize the payments to the Province provided for in the said agreement of any balance from proceeds of the sale or other disposition of the lands or any portion thereof, together with accrued unexpended simple interest thereon and of one-half of the consideration in the case of the sale, lease or other disposition of mining claims staked on such reserve, or of lands in which minerals are included or may exist or be supposed to exist; and
(3)	to provide that no disposition shall be made of water-power in any such Indian Reserve of a greater capacity than five hundred horse-power except by special agreement, and that the provisions of the Bed of Navigable Waters Act, Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1914, chapter 31, shall apply to grants of such lands or
Indian Reserve Lands
minerals heretofore or hereafter made under the Great Seal of Canada or otherwise under the direction of the government of Canada.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Will the minister tell us, before we go into committee, what designs he has on the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
No designs
whatever. This has always been a controversial subject between the province of Ontario and the Dominion. Probably if I read a memorandum that has been prepared on the matter it will give a synopsis of the situation:
1.	The respective rights of the Dominion of Canada and the provincce of Ontario in relation to Indian lands within the province first came before the Judicial committee of the Privy Council in 1888, when it was held (in St. Catharines' Milling Company vs. The Queen, 1888, 14 App. Cas. 46) that lands surrendered by the Indians to the Crown subsequent to Confederation belonged not to the Dominion, which had negotiated the treaty, but to the province.
2.	Fourteen years later the question again came before the Judicial committee in a slightly different form, in Ontario Mining Company, Limited, vs. Seybold, 1903, A.C. 73. To that appeal the Dominion was a party, but just before the argument an agreement between Mr. Blake, representing the province, and Mr. Newcombe, representing the Dominion, was entered into, and the latter took no part in the argument, which was followed by a judgment in effect confirming the conclusion arrived at in the earlier appeal.
3.	The agreement (known as "counsel's agreement'', and dated 7th July, 1902), provided that, without prejudice to the legal rights of either the province or the Dominion, and merely as a matter of convenience, the Dominion should, upon their surrender by the Indians, have power to dispose of lands included in reserves in Ontario, the Dominion to hold the proceeds subject to the rights of the province. It was further provided that the question whether this right of disposition by the Dominion should extend to the precious metals should depend upon the instruments and circumstances and law relevant to each particular piece of land.
4.	This agreement has been enacted upon and dispositions made by the Dominion, but no step has ever been taken to settle the legal position even as to ths surface and base metals, and the uncertainty as to the precious metals has stood in the way of the disposition of these, with the result that such precious metals as the reserves may contain have in fact not been dealt with, to the detriment both of the Indians, who would receive the benefit of the disposition, and of the province, which does not obtain the benefit of any taxation on the output of mines, which it might otherwise do.
5.	It was not until 1920 that the strictly legal position of lands in Indian reserves surrendered for sale was discussed before the Judicial committee. Then in a case from Quebec (Attorney General for Quebec vs. Attorney General for Canada, 1921, A.C. 401), it was held that a patent by the Dominion of lands included in a reserve and surrendered by the Indians in trust for sale was ineffective, since upon the surrender the title passed, not to the Dominion, but to the province. It is probable that the strictly legal position in relation to reserves in the province of Ontario is identical with that in Quebec, although practically the situation is altered by counsel's agreement. The statutory confirmation of this agreement would, however, be highly convenient to both the Dominion and the province, and obviously that confirmation should
rMr. C. A. Stewart.]
extend to the settlement of the uncertainty in relation to the precious metals.
6.	The geological formations in Ontario are such that precious and base metals ordinarily occur together and are only separated in the course of refinement. To deal with the precious metals consequently involves dealing also with the base metals, and the arrangement proposed by the present draft agreement is that upon the sale or other disposition of minerals lands one-half of the total proceeds should belong to the Dominion for the benefit of the Indians, and the other half to the Province.
7.	In addition to dealing with the minerals and to confirming counsel's agreement, the present draft agreement also contains a new provision that the capital sum received by the Dominion by way of consideration for the disposition of any interest in lands in reserves may be expended for the benefit of the Indians and that the province, on the extinction of Indian right, becomes entitled only to so much of the capital as may remain unexpended.
That is in brief a sketch of the difficulties the amending legislation has to cover and a statement of what the bill to be founded in this resolution proposes to do.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: I have not observed, Mr. Chairman, that there is any definite consent on the part of the Indians to the proposed agreement. Have they agreed to this? Some hon. member says they have no say in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
This has
been a very vexed question. It is largely one not affecting the Indians so much as affecting the dispute as to final ownership.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Between the provinces and
the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
It was I who made the
comment that I did not think the Indians
had any say because they are not affected. I do not see that they have the least concern as to where the legal title is, once it passes from the Indians. The Indian has a say, of course, before it passes from him. I was rather surprised to hear my hon. friend say that the Indians had agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I presume
the Indians would be better satisfied if they had the disposal of the money which comes from the sale of the land. After the sale of the lands all the proceeds are to be used in the interests of the Indians, unless a tribe of Indians becomes extinct, and there may be a small portion of the revenue coming from the land, which should go to the province.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
It is between the provinces and the Dominion, and not between the Indians and the Dominion at all. Do

Indian Reserve Lands
I get the real meaning of it? By reason of the judicial opinion of the Privy Council expressed back in the eighties, the surrender of Indian lands in provinces, after those provinces came into confederation, vested the title to the surrendered lands in the provinces instead of in the Dominion. Consequently some action in another form came before the Privy Council in 1902; and instead of giving judgment an arrangement was made between the counsel concerned, Mr. Blake and Mr. Newcombe, the basis of which arrangement is to be ratified and made law by this bill, in so far as Canada is concerned. Necessarily it will, as well, have to be made law by the provinces concerned. Therefore the only matter left to be understood is, what the arrangement is. Have I got the minister's words or his memorandum aright? -the arrangement in effect was this: That the lands, though the property of the province after surrender by the Indians, should be administered by the Dominion for the benefit of the Indians who surrendered it, and when the time arrived that there was an extinction of the Indians' rights by extinction of the tribe, or by some other means, if it ever occurred, the remainder left over should pass to the provincial government. I understood the minister to say it passed to the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Yes, my
hon. friend is right. Clause 7 reads:
In addition to dealing with the minerals and to confirming counsel's agreement, the present draft agreement also contains a new provision that the capital sum received by the Dominion by way of consideration for the disposition of any interest in lands in reserves may be expended for the benefit of the Indians and that the province, on the extinction of the Indian right, becomes entitled only to so much of the capital as may remain unexpended.
We have control of the money so long as there is any Indian in existence. We may dispose of the land and use it, if it is in the interest of the Indian, but when the Indian is extinct, and there is no further method by which the government can expend the money in the interests of that tribe, then the province becomes entitled to only so much of the capital as remains unexpended.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I do not know that I
understand it, and I would really like to. Do I understand that some of these grants of land were made by the British Crown to the Indians before confederation, and these Indians agreed to give up the title to the land?
205i
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil);:	I think
there were treaties in effect between the Indians and the representatives of the government.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: The minister means between the British Crown and the Indians. I think there is more in this than appears on the surface.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: I thought the land was reserved and not granted to the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: I said there were treaties made.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: But it involves the question of title. The question was as to whether the lands were granted to the Indians. I always understood that there were no grants but reservations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: If my hon. friend is correct in his interpretation the land is reserved to be set aside for the Indians and to be administered by the Crown.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
The title remaining in the
Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: It could not be a grant.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I have seen an agreement
between the government of Queen Victoria and the Indians, and the agreement was practically granting the lands to the Indians. I do not know the exact form in which it was drawn up, but I have never seen anything in the agreement which provided that any day the government could step in and say, "You cannot have this reserve any longer." The Indians have a title of some kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: There is no doubt that as long as there are any Indians the reserves which are set apart for the Indians are reserved for them. But what we are seeking to deal with is the case where the Indian has no longer any interest in the land.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Has the Indian agreed to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: If he is dead you cannot get his agreement. As long as he is alive he has an interest in it.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I suppose there will be concurrent legislation in the provinces. What is the proposition? Is the title to be in the Dominion?
Mr. STEWART Argenteuil): No. The title is not interfered with. The judgment of the Privy Council indicated that such title to the land as existed was probably in the province, but the land was reserved for the use
Indian Reserve Lands

of the Indians. We are making an arrangement whereby, when the land ceases to be any longer required for the use of the Indians, if that times comes, the province becomes entitled to what is left. Probably I should put it in this way: Under the terms of the agreement the Dominion government have control, and they may sell the lands and use the money under the provisions of the Indian Act and do what seems to be necessary in the interests of the Indians; but when the time comes that there are no more Indians of that particular tribe occupying that particular land, and there is no reserve left, the funds that may remain will go to the hands of the province.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Evidently the sale would be
made by the province and the proceeds of the sale would be handed over to the department for its administration on behalf of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: The sale would be made by the Dominion.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Then the provinces are agreed that the title for the purposes of this provision shall be in the Indians. They shall make the sale and use the money for the benefit of the Indians;-the title must be either in the Dominion or in the provinces, I understood the minister to say the title was really in the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: My hon. friend is raising the point as to who issues the title in the case of sale during the life of the Indians? .

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: We have full control to expend capital moneys derived from the sale. Mr. Biggar drafted this legislation, and he was consulted generally in connection with the agreement. Section 7, which I have just read covers it pretty well. The province comes in only when the tribe is extinct. When the extinction takes place, if there are any sums remaining from the proceeds of the sales of those lands, that money goes to the provinces. But we have complete control of the lands.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
One point is not very
clear to me. Section (1) speaks of lands being surrendered by the Indians "in order that they may be disposed of for the benefit of the band." What method is taken to get the surrender of the lands by the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
By a vote
of the band.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Unless by a vote they
voluntarily surrender the land, the government has no authority to sell it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: The Indian Act gives the government pretty wide authority, but in no case have we attempted to dispose of or to lease land unless we have had a majority vote of the band concerned.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
And this legislation is
not taking any further authority than the government now had, because it refers only to lands surrendered by the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
No.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I thoroughly understand
what the purport of the resolution is, and on its merits in general I have no adverse criticism to offer, but I really did not know before that the holding of the Privy Council applied to all the provinces. I thought this difficulty had arisen in connection with what is really known in law as the reversionary interest, in British Columbia alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
This does
Dot apply to all the provinces. This is an agreement between Ontario and the federal government.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: The minister's explanation applied to every province. That is what mystified me.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: I am sorry. I should have to deal separately with every province.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
This does not get over
the British Columbia trouble at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
No; I
would be glad if it would.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
We are not carried very far by this resolution. I had hoped that the minister had made a settlement of the question with all the provinces. It is in British Columbia that the trouble arises. Will the minister explain, if such is the situation to be cured in Ontario, what is the different one in British Columbia? In British Columbia the provincial government has always claimed the reversionary title, that is to say, in lay language, the title after the Indians' rights are extinct by extinction of the Indians themselves or otherwise; but in Ontario I did not know that any such claim was advanced, in the same sense at least as it is in British Columbia. What does British Columbia claim over and above what this decision held to be the right of Ontario?

Indian Reserve Lands

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Is the right
hon. gentleman speaking of the British Columbia government?

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
What is the trouble in
British Columbia? Is the situation there exactly what it has been in Ontario prior to this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Broadly
speaking, the situation has been this. The adjustment between the provincial government and the federal government as to the question of reversion, the administration required in the case of extinction of the Indians' rights, has been in dispute between the governments, and as my right hon. friend is aware, a commission was appointed to go very thoroughly into the question, 'both governments tentatively agreeing to accept the decision of that commission. The commission reported after a good length of time had been taken up in arriving at a decision, 'and the Indians are objecting to the commission's finding which recommends the sale of some of the lands that, the commission say, are not required by the tribes. That deals with the older reserves. But the root of the objection by the British Columbia Indian is his claim that he is entitled, not only to reversion, but to the whole of the area of British Columbia; that is, that his hereditary right has never been extinguished. That is the most serious objection in my opinion. The federal government for the past eighteen months have been endeavouring to reconcile the Indians, that is, to get some further consideration as regards the reserve question. But the other question is the real reason for the British Columbia Indian objecting to a settlement of almost any sort. There are foreshore rights, fishing rights and a number of other rights that, perhaps, we can adjust; but the bigger question that is raised by the friends of the British Columbia Indians themselves is the claim to the original title to the whole area known as British Columbia. I would not care to enter upon a discussion of that question this afternoon.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Do they claim the
whole province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Yes; they
say their title has never been extinguished.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
I hope the minister i3
losing more sleep over the national debt than he is over that question. I remember now very vividly the agitation for acknowledgement of the whole of British Columbia as being still the possession of the Indians.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Will the'right hon- member not wish the minister sound sleep in any event?

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: No; I think he ought to get the national debt down a little before he has a right to sleep soundly. That is the agitation, if I recall it correctly, headed by the Rev. Mr. O'Meara.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Not
"reverend"; he is a legal gentleman.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: I think he is both; and that is "some" combination. I will not bother discussing that, and the minister cannot be very busy if he occupies much of his time over it. He hardly appreciates the situation as I was endeavouring to lay it before him. I am, or at least I think the government ought to be, very anxious to get a settlement of that reversionary title claim in British Columbia. The question never was crucial in Ontario. It never was brought to the surface while I was connected with the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: It comes up now perhaps more acutely in connection with the finding of the commission.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
A commission which
looked into the matter brought in a report; the Dominion government were ready to abide by the report, but British Columbia was recalcitrant, and I must admit that I entirely failed to make any progress with the present premier of British Columbia. That, however, is no reason why the minister should not. I notice the premier announces that he is good friends with the Dominion government. I do not know what he is not getting; I notice he is getting an elevator in Prince Rupert and he is apparently going to fix rates in this parliament. Why can the minister not take advantage of this great friendship and secure the settlement of a question that is really crucial in British Columbia namely the reversionary question? It is thwarting, hampering the work in British Columbia all the time. It is big and difficult, and it is complicated. The minister has had two and a half years now, with his colleague from that part of the 'country, to settle the matter. Has he made any progress at all or has his experience been very much like my own?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
It is hardly fair to blame the provincial government for the delay at the moment. The provincial government has shown a disposition to meet us but there are a number of questions involved
Indian Reserve Lands

in addition to the reversionary right which it is difficult to settle. One of these difficulties arose in connection with the question of the fisheries. The federal government, controls that matter in most cases so that it was really not a departmental question. Our Indian wards are not satisfied and I have been endeavouring to appease them with the adjustment that has been made by the commission. They claim that in many cases they are entitled to consideration in relation to foreshore and fishing rights, which consideration they say they have not received under that award. We have been trying to adjust matters and to get the Indians to agree to the settlement, but I am bound to admit that some of their friends have given them bad advice. That has been the chief difficulty; were it not for the class of advice they have got I believe we could have a settlement of the matter in the near future.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
Does the
agreement with Ontario affect in any way the present status of the dispute between the Department of Indian Affairs and certain islands in the river St. Lawrence which were originally a, part of the St. Regis reservation? Some half dozen islands were held under 99-year leases at ridiculously low rentals.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Were they reserves?

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: Yes. About six or seven years ago these leases expired, and if I remember rightly the department took the ground that they were not renewable and refused' to renew them. Does this agreement with. Ontario contemplate any change in the status of that dispute with respect to those islands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
No. This
merely deals with the disposition of receipts from minerals and so on. The federal government has complete control of the management of the estate, if we may use that term, which is being operated in the interests of the Indian. So that any agreement of the character my hon. friend mentions would be dealt with departmentally; this would not touch it at all.

maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext: But it is not merely a matter of agreement, it is a matter of litigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN RESERVE LANDS
speechtext:
That may
be.	We frequently have difficulty about 
leases and matters of contract but this particular matter is simply one between the lessee and the government. It is not an inter-provincial matter at all.

Section agreed to.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Stewart (Argenteuil) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 191, for the settlement of certain questions between the governments of Canada and Ontario respecting Indian Reserve Lands.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of the Interior) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend section eight of the Northwest Territories Act, Revised Statutes, 1906, chapter 62, by adding to the subjects on which the Commissioner in Council may make ordinances as therein designated, the levying of an export tax on furs within the territories.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the minister state
fully the effect of this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The purpose is to impose a fur tax on pelts taken in the Northwest Territories. For some years, I understand, there has been an agitation to have this done. The provincial governments are now collecting a tax on pelts taken within the four western provinces and this legislation will put the territories which lie immediately north of those provinces upon the same basis and thus assist us to some extent in paying for the administration. That is all that the bill purports to do; it gives us authority to collect a tax on furs.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is the tax applicable only to furs exported?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, it refers to fur coming out of the territory.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Some of that fur would
be export fur, and some would not be exported. Does the word "export" in this connection refer to furs exported out of Canada or merely out of the territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Out of the
territory.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If they are exporters, yes; but usually they are not. Whoever ships furs out of the territory for sale or disposition will pay a tax thereon.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have been requested to
ask the minister to let this matter stand; an hon. member who wishes to discuss it is not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Any hon.
member can register his objection when the bill is under consideration. We are merely getting the legislation forward a stage and there will be plenty of opportunity for hon. members to discuss it later.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
have an opportunity on some other occasion to discuss it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes; this is merely to get the bill introduced.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to let us know what the rate of tax is to be, whether specific or ad valorem?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It varies
somewhat from the similar tax collected by the provinces, but is based on the value of the fur. I might read this list to my hon. friend: On each white or polar bear, $2; on each bear not specified, 40 cents; on each beaver, $1; on each fisher, $1.50; on each black fox, $5; on each blue fox, $2,50; on each cross fox, $1.50; on each red fox, 75 cents; on each silver fox, $5; on each white fox, $1.50; on each lynx, 75 cents; on each marten, $1; on each mink, 25 cents; on each muskrat, 5 cents; on each otter, $1; on each skunk, 10 cents; on each weasel, 3 cents; on each wolf, wolverine or coyote, nothing.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend
having told us what the tax is to be, it would be very interesting if he would let us have the average price which the trapper gets for these pelts, because I have no doubt the minister will thoroughly appreciate that the fur-exporting companies will just take the duty off the price they pay to the trapper. A very large number of trappers are Indians, and they will be taxed just to this extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will endeavour to get the information from our officers and furnish it when the bill is under discussion.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If the minister will answer another question it may save discussion later on. Perhaps he has some ground for distinguishing this proposed tax from, or perhaps it is consonant with, the
governmental declaration as to the non-taxation of the original products of the soil with a view to helping those engaged therein, whether by land or by sea. By proposing this taxation the -government is swallowing itself, and doing it very gracefully, because furhunting is an original activity of the Indians. On what grounds is this original activity to be taxed as against exemptions granted in other directions? Is it because there are no representatives of this primary production in the House, no votes to cajole, nothing to be done to keep the government in power when it ought to be put out?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon.
friend seems to discover a new mode of attack. This is not a new tax; surely my hon. friend knows that in the northern portions of the four provinces mentioned fur taxes are imposed. Instead of this being a detriment to the Indians we hope it will be of assistance to them. White trappers are going into the territories in ever-increasing numbers to the very great disadvantage of the Indians, so much so that we have to put a rather heavy license fee upon the white trappers in an endeavour to keep them out. The Indian is a most careful hunter with a view to conserving his food supply, but the white trapper does not exercise similar care. Consequently the cost of administration of the Northwest Territories, which is a vast area, is steadily increasing. This is the only country in which to my knowledge there is not such a tax. We think we are entitled to get this tax from the fur trappers in these territories.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
my hon. friend does not answer me at all. There is the policy of his government formally declared; here is the action. It is no argument to say that we have taxes on furs in other parts of the country. If he were putting the declared policy of the government into effect he would be taking those taxes off instead of extending them. But here we have a very novel idea seriously advanced by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Why not? Is
not this a matter of primitive production? The minister nods his head. He is right, of course it is. Did not the government say it was in favour of looking after primary production? The minister does not nod his head this time. Well, that is what the government say anyway, whether he nods his head or not. He points out that this is not a

Northwest Territories Act
new tax. Well, there were some old taxes on primitive productions, but some of them have been got rid of. Of course, it is 5 p.m. true that others have been imposed. Here, we have this tax on primitive production confined to certain areas, and now it is to be increased. The minister has not answered my query as to how his action jibes with the general policy of the government. I do not think he can. But he has given us this new thought-that any specific industry is helped by taxation! Let us help the Indian. How? By putting a tax on everything that he produces. That is all the minister is doing to help the Indian. Well, that is an extraordinary way of helping the red man. But the trouble is, it does not help. My hon. friend says that there are too many white trappers in the Northwest Territories. If so, there is a way of dealing with them instead of taking money out of the pockets of the Indians, for this tax means that for every bear, mink or marten the Indian catches he will make that much less money. If the minister really wanted to help the Indians he would exact such license fees from, and impose such regulations on, white trappers as would preserve these areas to the Indians. But for the minister to say, "We are helping the Indians by taxing them on their furs," -well, I had hopes of better things from my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
While the
fur the Indian captures is important, it is not so important as the food question in the northwest country. Our Migratory Birds Act, for instance, has caused a very considerable amount of suffering on account of making it impossible for them to shoot in the spring. It is a question of food with the natives, rather than making money out of the fur Fur used in the territory will bear no tax at all. The Eskimo is clothed entirely in fur, with very few exceptions; there are a few, of course, in better financial circumstances who can buy woollen clothing. The Indian's dress, generally speaking, is of fur, and his chief difficulty is his food supply, so much so that we have had to supply them, as did my hon. friends opposite, with food and clothing from time to time. It is the white man who makes the huge profits that are being made to-day in the fur business. It is the white trapper who is jeopardizing the Indian's means of existence to a very serious degree, and who forces this government, and will force succeeding governments, to spend more and more money in policing the territory in the interests of the Indian. We have to do that TSir Henry Drayton.]
unless we are going to spend more and more money in maintaining the Indians. In view of that, I think I am asking only a reasonable tax on this business which is done largely by white trappers brought into that country by the Hudson's Bay people. These trappers come up there by boat in the fall and engage in trapping along the northern coast and to the northwest, and come out again the following year. The Indians will not suffer to any appreciable extent by the imposition of this tax.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no intention of
speaking on the virtue or lack of virtue in the tax itself. Men more familiar with the fur trade may do that, but I would like to ask the minister in regard to one rather interesting point involved, and that is the question of taxation without representation. As I understand it, the Northwest Territory has no representation, either federal or provincial, and as I understand the British constitution, which is the Canadian constitution, no one shall be subject to taxation without representation. That has always been the great principle, no taxation without representation, and I would like to ask the minister how he reconciles this tax on the products produced in an unorganized territory by people who have not the franchise wtih that great principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We could
easily adjust that difficulty by granting them the franchise.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Who, the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No. I
have just been trying to point out to my hon. friend that the Indian will not be seriously affected by the imposition of this tax; I was referring to the white man. Some of the Indians do make a very considerable amount of money trapping, but not generally speaking.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Are the Indians exporting fur at all, or do they sell the fur in Canada? Alaska is pretty close there, and I was wondering whether they shipped their furs across the line or sold them in Canada. What are the white trappers doing in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The fur
pack goes out of that country in three different directions. Around the western coast it goes out by the Hudson bay, usually by Hudson bay boats. The Hudson's Bay Company sends in a vessel every year with supplies for their posts around by the coast of

Northwest Territories Act
Alaska and in the northern waters, and leaves trappers along the coast. The third way is down the Mackenzie river, and out by Edmonton. Those are the three directions by which the fur we propose to tax is exported.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does the minister mean
exporting when the fur is sold to go outside the territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not quite clear about one thing, a constitutional question. I presume the Northwest Territories are a part of. Canada, and I thought there was a provision in the British North America Act by which the product of any part of Canada should not have a duty placed upon it with reference to any other part. Whether that strictly applies to export or not, I do not know. I would have some doubt -as to the power to impose a duty upon products going from one part of Canada to another. It is perfectly clear a duty could be imposed upon the products of Canada going to a foreign country, going out of Canada as a whole, but whether it is against the letter or not, it is certainly against the spirit of the British North America Act that you should impose what is really a duty as against the other provinces seeking to obtain the prdoucts of any one province. I wonder if that had the consideration of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I confess
this is a new thought to me. The provinces have the right to impose a tax on fur and they exercise it. If that is the basic industry my hon. friend is worrying about, the provinces undoubtedly have that right and they exercise it. The Northwest Territories, however, are administered as a territorial unit. Whether that confers authority to impose taxation I am unable to say for the moment, but I will look into the matter.

maintopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The point I was making
has no reference to the authority of the territories but to the authority of this parliament. I assume that an export duty can be placed on lumber going from New Brunswick into any other province; and that an export duty may be put on, let us say, iron ore going from Ontario into any other province. But certainly the British North America Act never contemplated the possibility of a
Supply-Tax Collections

system of interprovincial duties even under federal organization. The point only occurred to me a few moments ago, and I should like to look into it further. I would think the minister would require to give the matter very close attention, because it is a much more important affair than the mere size of the tax. It is a question of whether or not the thing can be done at all. In this House I rather think we rush into legislation that will cost many thousands of dollars, and allow the matter to be resolved afterwards by the submission of questions to the Supreme Court and by appeals to the Privy Council, when we might save a good deal of time and misplaced energy by simply giving a little thought to these matters before we enter into them. Section 121 of the British North America Act provides that:
All articles of the growth, produce or manufacture of any one of ithe provinces shall, from and after the union, be admitted free into each of the other provinces.
That is entirely inconsistent with the idea of an interprovincial export duty. The only question that remains is whether the Northwest Territories are at all in the status of a province. I have not had time to look into the subsequent acts which gave them the status they now enjoy. I understand they are included now as part of Canada and perhaps the reason referred to might apply.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Stewart (Argenteuil) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 192, to amend the Northwest Territories Act.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the first time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting, Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee of Supply.
Mr. W. C. GOOD (Brant) moved in amendment, seconded by Mr. Brown:
That all the words after " that " be omitted, and the following substituted therefor:
Whereas it has been alleged in the public press of Canada that if an inquiry were instituted, some interesting information and astonishing facts, showing how the treasury of Canada failed to receive revenue intended for it, would be disclosed to the taxpayers of the Dominion; and
Whereas, for instance, it has been alleged in the press that cheques totalling about $1,700,000, representing the income and business profits taxes of three well known concerns in Ontario, were received by the Department of Finance in March, 1921, but were not deposited until December 6 of that year; and

Whereas a number of similar specific allegations have been made in the press; and
Whereas it has been alleged in the House of Commons on May 27 of this year, that in the case of a certain corporation the treasury of the Dominion seems to have lost in one year about $800,000 to which it was entitled;
Therefore, in the opinion of this House it is expedient that the standing committee on Public Accounts be and same is hereby instructed to investigate the methods by which the business profits and income taxes, especially in the case of large concerns, have been assessed and collected.
He said:	I referred to one of the matters
mentioned' in the amendment on the 27th, May, as stated in the text, and at the conclusion of the debate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and the Prime Minister particularly, assured me that the matters which I submitted to the House, could be taken up before the Public Accounts committee. At least such was my understanding of the assurance given on that occasion. Subsequently I made an effort to secure a meeting of the Public Accounts committee at which Mr. Breadner, Commissioner of Taxation, might be questioned on certain matters. I have exercised a great deal of ingenuity between that date and the present in order to secure a meeting of the committee, but have failed, and it is for that reason that I now ask the House to instruct the committee to take cognizance of this and other similar matters I have been told that I should bring a specific charge of wrong doing against some official. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it must be apparent to the House that after it has been claimed by the Acting Minister of Finance and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and all those concerned, that the files and information concerning these matters, are confidential, it is practically impossible for anyone at this stage, to make a definite and specific charge. Section 14 of chapter 11 of the Business Profits War Tax reads as follows:
"No person employed in the service of His .Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act. Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable on summary, conviction to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars."
This I presume is the basis of the statements made by the Acting Minister of Finance and the ex-M'inister of Finance in regard to the impossibility or the difficulty of securing any information. Reference was also made on a former occasion to the fact that some information must have leaked out. I think it must be apparent to all, and I think we

Supply-Tax Collections
may take it for granted, that the information upon which the Globe articles were based, upon which I base nay own case, leaked out through some of the officials. Why did they violate this particular section of the act, and inform parties outside of what they were pledged not to divulge? My conclusion is that some of the officials must have felt that their obligation to the country was greater than their obligation to observe the law. I am not the guardian of their consciences and do not wish to judge them in this matter. However, they have run the risk of dismissal and penalty for violating the law for certain reasons which they must have considered sufficient.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
['As this motion requires the unanimous consent of the House, it would require to stand until Wednesday when the order is called, when that consent may be given.
Motion stands.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.45 u.m.
Tuesday, June 17, 1924']

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What evidence has my hon.
friend that the information was given out from the Income Tax department?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I take it that such must
have been the case. Perhaps I might, if I were so disposed, give my hon. friend more particular information. I am satisfied, however, from what you might call general reasoning and very specific information of a confidential character, that such has been the case. Il seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the question which we have before us is in its general aspects one of considerable importance. Is parliament not entitled to know how its own acts are being administered? We have been told that these files are confidential, and that therefore no one can find out what assessments have been made, or anything about assessments and collections. I do not see how we can possibly accept that conclusion. It seems to me a most extraordinary, anomalous, absurd and untenable position to assert that parliament cannot find out how its own laws are being administered. I have taken some little trouble to look into the matter of the powers of parliament in this particular regard, and I venture to submit a statement thereon to the House. First in regard to the obligations which are involved in the present Income Tax Act, I refer to Plaxton and Varcoe, page 254, where I find the following:
Income tax returns are official documents and generally speaking the Crown cannot be compelled to produce them in court if the responsible officer of the department states upon oath that their production would be contrary to the public interest. Upon an application made by the liquidator of a company for the production of returns the court in the exercise of its discretion refused the application on an affidavit being filed that in the opinion of the Board of Inland Revenue such production would be prejudicial to the public interest. In an action for damages for slander it was held that the defender was not entitled to the production of the pursuer's income tax returns.
This shows, I think, that no person in the government service shall communicate any
information to any person not legally entitled, that the Crown has a right to treat the income tax returns as official documents, and that they cannot be compelled to produce them in court. But that is an entirely different matter from the right of parliament or a committee of parliament to call witnesses and secure information. I refer to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, page 70, where I find the following:
The Senate and House of Commons have the right, inherent in them as legislative bodies, to summon and compel the attendance of all persons, within the limits of their jurisdiction, as witnesses, and to order them to bring with them such papers and records as may be required for the purpose of an inquiry.
At page 74 of the same authority, I find the following:
No witness before either House of parliament or a committee of either House can excuse himself from answering any proper question that may be put to him. While the law of parliament demands the disclosure of the evidence it recognizes to the fullest extent the principle on which the witness is excused from making such disclosure in the ordinary courts of Justice and protects him against the consequences which might otherwise result from his testimony, the rule of parliament being that no evidence given in either House can be used against the witness in any other place without the permission of the House.
At page 75, continuing the same line of thought, I find the following:
The experience of parliament has shown that in the majority of cases select committees are the be3t tribunals for examining witnesses and accordingly it will be found on reference to parliamentary records, evidence is taken whenever practicable before select committees.
At page 480, I find the following:
It is usual in both houses to give committees special authority to send for witnesses or documentary evidence.
At page 482, we find:
In the session of 1891 the committee of privileges and elections to whom was referred a very important inquiry, reported that one of the witnesses refused to place under the immediate control of the committee certain documents, which he (had produced. His conduct was reported to the House, and he was ordered to deliver all accounts and papers to the clerk of the House. He complied at once with the order, and the committee had consequently full control of the documents in question.
I quote from page 74 of Bourinot, the following:
In view of certain prosecutions and suits, criminal and civil instituted by the Department of Justice subsequent to inquiries before the committee of Privileges, and in committee of Public Accounts in 1891, the House ordered in 1892 that all clerks and stenographers who were in the employment of the House, and in attendance on the said committees, "should attend, when required before the courts and give evidence as to the statements made upon oath, and produce all books and papers used before the said committees"; and it was distinctly laid down in the same resolution that the House, "while waiving its privileges in these
Supply-Tax Collections

particular cases with the view of eliciting all the facts and obtaining substantial justice in the premises, does not in any sense give up its well established and undoubted rights, whenever it may deem it in the public interest hereafter at any time to protect all witnesses examined before this House or any committee thereof in respect of anything that may be said by them in their evidence, and to refuse permission to any clerk or officer of the House or shorthand writer employed to take minutes of evidence before the House or any committee thereof to give evidence elsewhere in respect to any proceedings or any examination had at the bar or before any committee of the House."
In, Hansard of 1892, volume 1, at page 1290, Sir John Thompson quotes Cushing, a great American authority, as follows:
A Witness before the House of Parliament cannot excuse himself from answering any question that may be put to him (with a single exception presently to be noticed) on the ground that the answer would subject him to an action or expose him to a criminal proceeding, or be the means of divulging the secret of his client communicated to him in professional confidence, or be ary breach of a judicial oath as grand juror, etc., some of which would be sufficient grounds of excuse in a court of justice. This difference between proceedings in parliament and in the ordinary courts has been established upon grounds of public policy and is considered to be fundamentally essential to the efficacy of a parliamentay inquiry, but while the law of parliament thus demands the disclosure of the evidence, it recognises to the fullest extent the principle upon which the witness is excused from making such diclosure in the ordinary courts of justice and protects him from the consequence which might otherwise result from his testimony.
And so forth. I have some other references, but it is not necessary to quote them on the present occasion. I want to mention in conclusion the case of Mr. R. C. Miller in 1913 which is contained in the Journals of the House, pages 274 to 278. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will recall this because he seconded a number of motions made at that time. Mr. Miller refused to answer certain questions; he was called before the bar of the House where, on advice of counsel, he refused to answer the questions, and he was imprisoned until the end of the session.
All this evidence, it seems to me, shows an undoubted right of parliament to inquire into any matters such as have been claimed to be confidential and such as are necessary to inquire into in order to find out how the Business Profits War Tax Act and the Income Tax Act are being interpreted and applied. I may take it, therefore, that there is no doubt as to the power of parliament in this connection.
The other day when the Income Tax Act was under consideration, I had prepared an amendment to the act, but I was unfortunately unable to be present and left it in the hands of another member. But under conditions existing on the evening when the

matter was under discussion the amendment was not submitted. I should like to read it to the House now:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to interfere with the privileges of the House or of any committee thereof in ordering the production of returns, statements, reports, memoranda or writings made by any corporation, co-partnership or individual under this act, or to prevent the House or any committee thereof from compelling witnesses to answer questions or give information.
As a matter of fact, I was informed by the law clerk of the House, after a very lengthy discussion, that this amendment was not necessary, although there would be no harm in inserting it in the act, because it was generally understood that parliament has the right at any time to inquire into these matters, to compel the production of papers and to compel witnesses to answer questions even though those answers might incriminate them in the ordinary courts.
In view of these facts, I claim that the committee ought to be open to investigate these matters. I have been asked by the chairman of the committee to make a specific charge. I have told him that I can make no charge more specific than I have already made, and apparently that is not judged sufficient to warrant an investigation. As I said before, I am, therefore, compelled to ask the House to issue instructions to the committee to have this matter investigated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The operative part of
the hon. member's resolution, the last paragraph states:
It is expedient that the standing committee on Public Accounts be and same is hereby instructed to investigate the methods by which the business profits and income taxes, especially in the case of large concerns, have been assessed and collected.
This is open to the interpretation that all that the committee could investigate would be the principles upon which assessments and taxes are arrived at and how, after being arrived at, they are pressed for collection. Does the hon. member intend that the committee shall be empowered, and that its duty shall be, to investigate the actual facts relevant to the correct assessment, the business affairs themselves and what the assessment should be, in a word, the details of the business or of the individual concerned?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is quite possible that the
wording is not the happiest in this respect and, perhaps, not as clear as it ought to be. I may, however, answer my right hon. friend by saying that the idea that I hoped to convey was that the committee should inquire into, not only the facts in so far as those facts
seem relevant to establish certain principles of interpretation and method, but the general interpretation and the general application of the law.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That does not answer my *question. Is the committee to be empowered to summon the man taxed, the officer of the company before it, and to get at the details of the business so as to enable the committee to decide whether that man or firm was rightly taxed or not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

I think we shall have to leave

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It will not have any
power except what this resolution gives it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope that if the resolution
does not convey the powers that have just been described, it can be amended so as to convey ample powers of inquiry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Into the individual
case?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes; and I shall be very glad
to have any amendment to the operative part of the resolution to bring about that result.
I can assure my right hon. friend that I have no desire to limit the inquiry; in fact, I am very anxious that any question which is relevant should be inquired1 into by the committee.
If I may further trespass on the time of the House, there is first the question of the interpretation of the law, and I have in mind particularly a dispute which, after the debate the other day, I got into with Mr. Breadner over the interpretation of the Business Profits War Tax Act. I may be wrong and he may be right, or he may be wrong and I may be right, but the matter of interpretation ought to be cleared up in the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That would be a legal
matter, would it not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I presume it would, to some
extent, although I think parliament has power over such matters. Further than that, there is the question of actual facts in regard to certain assessments. I should like, for instance, that the committee should take cognizance of the particular assessment that I submitted to the House on a previous occasion and also should inquire into those other assessments that have been referred to in press despatches. In addition to the matters referred to on a previous occasion, and after
the former debate, I received a letter from a man in Toronto whom I do not know at all. He marks it "private and confidential", and therefore I shall not disclose his name. This letter is to the effect that the evasions of the law in Toronto have been legion. He gives me to understand that he knows of numerous cases of what, for want of a better term with which to describe them, I must call evasions, to say the least. I know nothing about this, but it seems to me that the committee might well take cognizance of the matter; my correspondent offers to send me a list of the concerns which he has in mind. He says:
If you decide to go on with this I can furnish you with a list of names.
I do not wish to prolong the discussion further at the present time. I am anxious however that this matter, which has received a good deal of attention in the press and otherwise and about which there is a good deal of talk, should be cleared up; and apparently the only place where that can be done is before the Public Accounts committee.
I therefore urge that the matter be turned over to that committee for such inquiry as they may deem fit. As I said before, if the operative part of the resolution is not worded in such a way as to give to the committee the full and necessary powers to enable them to establish the facts and secure the information that is required, then I should like to see someone who may have better legal qualifications than I, amend the resolution to make it effective.
Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland):
I do not intend to discuss the merits of this resolution but I desire to refer briefly to the statement of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), that he had approached the chairman of the Public Accounts committee and used every ingenuity to have a meeting of that committee called to consider this matter. I happen to be the chairman of the Public Accounts committee, and I may say that when the hon. member approached me I called his attention to the tact that, after all, the powers of the Public Accounts committee are somewhat limited. We receive our powers from parliament and they are stated in a resolution which reads:
That the select standing committee of this House shall severally be empowered to examine end inqill'o into all such matters and things as may be referr=d to them by the House, etc.
We have had the Auditor General's report referred to us, but the matter which the hon. gentleman desired to have investigated was not included among the subjects that had
Supply-Tax Collections

been referred to the committee. I asked him whether he had any charge to make and he said he had not; he only desired to investigate into the methods of administration. It occurred to me that this was rather a wide field to enter upon:	It would necessitate an
investigation into the methods of administration of the Department of Finance, of the Customs department, of the Marine department, of the Department of Justice if the same should be demanded by any member of parliament. It did not appeal to me, therefore, as being particularly a matter which could come within the province of the Publics Accounts committee, a committee which after all, as its name signifies, is a body whose duty it is to examine into public accounts and not to inquire into public methods of administration. In offering this explanation, I do not think that my hon. friend intended to reflect upon my opposition to his proposal in itself; the only question was as to whether we had the power to investigate a matter which had not been referred to the Public Accounts committee, a matter which was not one of public accounts but one that had to do with methods of administration.
So far as I am concerned, I desire that the Public Accounts committee shall be given, not ill-considered directions, but well-defined instructions upon which to act. I think this matter opens up a vast field, and for myself I want specific instructions from the House as to how far we are to keep faith with the taxpayers of the country. We have undertaken to keep secret certain matters in connection with various businesses throughout the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That being so, is the Public Accounts committee now to investigate into the private affairs of every concern in Canada or of every individual? Is that to be its function or not? Without discussing the merits of the case that has been brought forward by the hon. member, I desire to have the considered judgment of the House on this question, for I am of the opinion that it is a matter of supreme importance for us to know how far we are to proceed under the circumstances. If we are to adopt such a proposal as this it is going to change the whole scope of the committee as we have so far understood it. Are we prepared to go as far as this implies? If the House directs that the Public Accounts committee shall investigate all these cases, the committee will of course do so. But we should have specific instructions before undertaking anything of the kind.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance):
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As will be found in the report
in Hansard of the evening session of May 27, when my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) made some reference to methods of collecting income tax, it was then stated on behalf of the government that if any hon. gentleman desired to make any charges relating to the administration of the act such charges would be investigated immediately and those who preferred them would be given an opportunity of appearing before the Public Accounts committee. I have listened to the resolution that has been presented to the House and, as I construe it, it seems that the hon. gentleman desires an inquiry into the method of administration of the department; I do not understand that he proposes to go into the details of the business of every man in this House or in the country. It is reasonable that hon. members who were not in this House when the legislation governing the administration of the Income Tax and the Business Profits Tax Acts were enacted should have an opportunity of inquiring generally into the method of administering the law. I desire now to draw to their attention the provisions of that law as it stands. Section 14 of the Business Profits War Tax Act, chapter 11 of the statutes of 1916, is as follows:
14. No person employed in the service of His Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act. Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable on summary conviction to a penality not exceeding two hundred dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the Acting Minister of Finance interpret that to mean that the officials may not be called before the committee or before parliament and be compelled to give information on these points?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am quoting the law as it
is; and the same thing appears in the Income War Tax Act, section 11 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1917. I want to give to my hon. friend the views of parliament of the time when this legislation was enacted; not the views of any individual but the unanimous opinion of parliament at that time including both sides of the House. When the legislation was before the House on August 8, 1917, Mr. Carvell, the member for Carle-ton, asked the Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, what course the government intended to pursue regarding the publication of details of taxation under the business profits war tax. I fancy Mr. Carvell asked

Supply-Tax Collections
that question because there was considerable opposition here and there to the giving out of details of people's business; business and professional men, farmers and others do not care to have the details of their business made known to their neighbours and everyone else.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Farmers have no
secrets.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There were farmers in the
House at that time, and they had the same objection. This is what Sir Thomas White answered:
When the Business Profits War Tax Act, whieh was introduced in 1916, was under consideration, the statement was made that returns would be brought down provided a resolution of the House was passed asking for such information. It was thought inadvisable that details of private business should be given. There seems to be a consensus of opinion that such details should not be made public.
That was Sir Thomas' view as to the consensus of opinion of the House at that time. Then he goes on:
My own view is that a member asking that information of a confidential nature should be brought down and made public, should lay a foundation, indicating that the assessment had not been properly made. Then, if such (position were prima facie sustained in the argument, the government would, I think, be justified in bringing down the information.
But Sir Thomas laid it down that first the member should make out a prima facie case. He communicated with the High Commissioner to ascertain from the Chancellor of the Exchequer what was the practice in Great Britain, and this was the reply by cablegram:
That under no circumstances would they permit the publication of detailed information relating to the business of individuals, firms and companies carrying on business in the United Kingdom and subject to the excess profits tax.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the minister understand that anybody in this House is proposing the publication broadcast of details of people's business? I do not propose it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am just making it dear, Mr. Speaker, that if such information was brought before a committee of the House it would be accessible to the newspaper reporters and would be scattered broadcast. But I was going to say that this is a new parliament, and if hon. members are not satisfied with the act and want to amend it, they are at liberty to proceed accordingly. But the government have no desire to keep back information in so far as it can be given under the act, amf therefore we have no objection to the resolution offered by my hon. friend, as I understand it, to bring before the Public Accounts committee inquiry into the administration of the act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope the minister
remembers that the hon. member said that that was just what he did not intend. It is pretty hard to ask the House to accept a resolution as meaning something which its mover says it does not mean.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am dealing
only with the resolution as it is before the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
