speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Outside of the recitals, Mr. Speaker, the amendment amounts to very little. I never liked these amendments, worded in such a form as to assume a very threatening and important aspect but really to contain nothing. The hon. member (Mr. Good), in answer to a question which I put to him, intimated that he intended that the amendment should empower the committee to inquire into any business whatever with a view to ascertaining the correctness of the assessment that had been made against it in any year; in a word, that the amendment intended to expose the affairs of whatever business might be under the suspicion of any member of the committee. He must have been somewhat surprised to find the Acting Minister of Finance state to him that the amendment meant nothing of the sort, and that because it meant nothing of the sort he intended to let it go; in a word, he intended to let the amendment pass by like the idle wind, just as the government lets many a motion go by on the assumption that it means nothing and will not do any harm.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: How could a committee investigate methods of assessment and collection without looking into some individual cases?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know, but the
unfortunate part of this amendment is that it does not say they will investigate anything. It says they will inquire into the methods; that is to say, I suppose, they could summon the chief officer and ask him what his methods were, and having got his methods, the organization that is under him, the general plan and scheme of assessment and collection, they could debate that, and I presume make a report to the House upon it. I know that is just what is in the mind of
Supply-Tax Collections

the acting minister, and he will dispute me now if I am wrong. That is the whole compass of the amendment as accepted by the acting minister. What an awful farce this is! What an awful farce! If the hon. member wants the Public Accounts committee empowered to inquire into and expose the affairs of businesses, let him say so in his amendment, or get one of his friends to do so -they cannot do so now in an amendment to this amendment, but the hon. member himself should have said so, and then the House would have had something to deal with. Now we are simply wasting time. This amendment, if it passes, is accepted by the government just because it is innocuous. It is a fraud on the House of Commons. It will not get anywhere; it will lead to no investigation; it is merely a method of evading the subject. What is the use of the hon. member saying, I am prepared to accept an amendment? You cannot move an amendment. He has brought something before the House that means nothing, but I presume it will enable someone to go out and say: We proposed that the committee should know all these facts; and enable someone on the government side to say: We accept the amendment from the Progressive party.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member suggest that that was the motive underlying the motion?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not know what the motive was. I will have to leave the suggestion as to it to my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: But surely he is sincere in the matter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Well, if he is, he is taking a strange method of getting anywhere. He gets nowhere by this amendment. The hon. member must recognize that from the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Will the
right hon. gentleman suggest a method that would get action?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know that I
have been constituted a tutor to the hon. member for Brant. When I have a course to pursue in the House, I put my course in plain language.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It might
help hon. members who are anxious to get this action.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am afraid hon. members are helpless. They have gone so far, there is no use suggesting anything. If the hon. member wanted me as counsel he might have come to me before. I had no notice whatever of this amendment; I had no idea it was coming up. Now, in the fon" in which it is before the House it is innocuous, and for the reason that it is innocuous the government accepts it, and for no other reason whatever. Nothing in the way of a motion in this House gets such a warm welcome from the administration as one that means nothing, and that is the reason for the splendid welcome that the hon. member's motion got from the Acting Minister of Finance.
Now as respects this part of the House. We are responsible for the legislation which is on the statute books. We take full responsibility for it; we believe it is the right legislation. However, if this government does not believe it is the right legislation, it is the responsibility of this government to propose an amendment. The House is quite competent to change the act, if in the judgment of the government it should be changed. We do not think it is in the interest of the country that there should be this exposure of private affairs. We believe these taxes must be collected on much the same principle as other taxes are collected. Officials must be provided, there must be supervision by members of the government, there must at the same time be availability of facts on any allegation of wrongdoing or malfeasance of office. These are the principles that we thought correct. We did not believe that any member of this House had any right to expose before the country any single feature of one of these details, unless it has been brought out in the regular way with all opportunity for disclosing the surrounding circumstances and presenting the other side of the case. I never thought it was honourable to throw before the country one exposed fact or allegation of fact. Hon. members on the other side thought differently, and wherever they could get even a rumour or allegation of fact-as for example in the Riordon case-they flaunted it before the country when they knew there was no opportunity for full disclosure, or that all the surrounding circumstances could be known. If any hon. member feels that the system should be different I would welcome a motion placing before this government the responsibility of establishing a different system. We took the responsibility when we were in office. I know of no reason why this government should evade it; and if hon. members to my left

Supply-Tax Collections
feel that there should be full disclosure of the facts of individual businesses, so that individual members of the House could determine whether assessments were right or were wrong, whether the terms were right or were wrong, then let an hon. member move to that effect and let the government take its position. But I am a little impatient of motions which simply evade the whole question and give the opportunity to the government to evade if.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely opposed to this amendment for the simple reason that I do not think it is fair to business men that such an amendment should be passed. I know a large number of business firms in Vancouver, who call in a chartered accountant, every six months, and have their books audited. When they have this done they give notice to the income tax office and an officer is sent down. He checks over the firm's accounts and the assessment is based on that showing. But the information so afforded is given with the direct understanding that it is confidential. That being so, why should other people be allowed to have this information to satisfy their idle curiosity, and in many cases that is the motive which prompts them to ask for an amendment of this kind. I think if the House adopts any such amendment it will make a very great mistake. In my opinion those who framed the Income Tax Act used good judgment, and the government has no right now to interpret it in such a way as to permit the disclosure of the business of any firm to the public. As the law now stands that is not done. If I had any criticism to offer in connection with this affair, it would be that in my opinion the salaries paid to the officers in charge of the Income Tax branch are not in keeping with the responsibility which devolves upon them. However, that is for the government to say.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I merely wish to make this
explanation. I was not in the House when the amendment was read from the chair and I have never seen it. Therefore I do not feel in a position to offer any remarks in respect to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think the member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) totally misconceives the idea held by the mover of this amendment; he (Mr. Good) does not want to inquire into the details of anyone's business. At the same time if cor-206
porations or individuals are not paying the taxes they should, there ought to be some way of ascertaining the facts, and whether there is anything wrong or not. maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

Is the House ready for
the question?

speechtext:

that I have not the right to speak again.

speechtext:

of the House the hon. member's wish may be granted.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is important to make
clear to the House particularly in view of the remarks of my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. McBride) just exactly what the amendment proposes. The leader of the Progressive party may be interested in learning the substantive part of the resolution which is as follows:
That in the opinion of this House it is expedient that the standing committee on Public Accounts be and the same is hereby instructed to investigate the methods by which the business profits and income taxes, especially in the case of large concerns, have been assessed and collected.
My hon. friend will see that that does not necessitate the disclosure of private business or the business of individual firms. If it did occasion such disclosure it would occasion a

Supply-Tax Collections

violation of the section of the statute which says:
No person employed in the service of His Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act. Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars.
It does not follow that became the business of individual firms may not be disclosed before the Public Accounts committee there may not be need for this resolution. There is, I think, in the minds of a good many considerable doubt as to the methods being emploj'ed in 'assessing taxes. For example, to what extent account is being taken of watered stock, how exceptions are arrived at and matters of that sort. I think it would be very much in the public interest to have doubts of that kind removed, and for that reason the government is quite prepared to accept the amendjment which has been moved. It may well he that the Commissioner of Taxation is proceeding in accordance with methods that will commend themselves to the judgment of the House. It is possible that in some particulars methods may be employed which would not be countenanced if the House were fully aware of them. In any event there appears to be doubt, in the minds of some persons as to the methods that are being followed, and if the course suggested by the amendment will help to remove doubts of the kind I should think a reference to the Public Accounts committee would serve a useful purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if he understands that the Public Accounts committee has no power to inquire into any particular case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Public
Accounts committee, like every other committee of the House, is subject to the laws of the land. The Public Accounts committee can operate within the scope of its authority, but it cannot violate any provisions of existing statutes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know that I can usefully add very much to what I said on the 27th May. I think I made my position very plain. There may be some hon. gentlemen, however, in the House now who were not in the House at that time. I invited discussion then. I invite it now; that is provided those in whose hands the good faith of this country now is reposed desire to break faith. I have

nothing to fear from investigation. It so happens that at present I am not in any way the keeper of the country's good faith. Attacks were made by gentlemen across the floor which were absolutely without foundation, which attacks I could not answer, because I could not keep faith on the one hand and give an answer on the other. Yes, the attacks were made with impunity, because the authors of these attacks thought I would have enough decency and honour to preserve the secrets of the department which were within my knowledge. Attacks were made on me indeed, by gentlemen who should have been very much interested in seeing that the proper secrets of the ratepayers were held inviolate.
The question is entirely one for this government. I am perfectly prepared tomorrow to go into an investigation, which would have to do with the only things that would be useful in a case of that kind, namely: What was done here and what was done there, what this man paid and what he ought to have paid. I am perfectly willing to go into it to-morrow morning. It is not for me to say. When I was keeping the conscience of the department I believed in keeping faith. Gentlemen across the floor were making attacks which they did not believe in, which they knew were wrong, which their own Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) deprecated when he took occasion in this House to say that he never associated himself with them, and attacks which my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) said this session he never associated himself with. But these attacks were made, and if attacks of this character are to be made, the only logical thing to do is just what the hon. member moving this resolution (Mr. Good) desires done. His idea is that you can do nothing useful here unless you find out concretely what was done. That is the thought of everybody. Was there a charge made against me in that campaign as to theory and as to principle? Not at all. The charge was specific having regard to specific taxes and specific individuals; and every one knows that the only successful way in which you can ascertain how an act has worked out, is to apply to it those very principles in question. Every one knows that. I am quite free to make that admission now. On the other hand, it is a good deal better that scurrilous attacks should be made and put up with, rather than that politicians should suffer, or that the business of the country should suffer. I am quite prepared to admit that, and I am quite willing to admit that the legislation which is now on the statute

books is the legislation of every civilized country in the world that desires to carry on, of every government that desires to see business carried on properly, of every administration which does not want to expose its business men to the venom of the busybody, or perchance to the blackmailer, by divulging to any one who asks for it, the business secrets of the organization.
Just think what the converse would mean. What chance would business men have if a stronger competitor could get information as to the inside of all his business, his results and the like, and know just exactly where to squeeze him. There are a lot of businesses, particularly to-day where the accounts show results which are not obtained entirely by the application of strict business principles, businesses where losses have taken place, where things are not going in the way they ought to be going-hundreds of them-and why? By reason of writing off depreciation and other similar charges. Just see what it means. If the results of the patient, painstaking stocktaking of a concern under these circumstances were made public, what would it mean? A wealthier or stronger concern would be able to see exactly how close that company was to insolvency and would be able to calculate, as a matter of days, if certain cuts were made, how that competitor could be put out of the way. That is just how it would work out. These are a few of the reasons why all countries that have any serious interest in business want these things kept in such a way that business can still be carried on.
The Prime Minister suggests the necessity of this investigation on account of watered stock. Is that suggestion not ridiculous? Any member of this House in five minutes can satisfy himself on the point as to what is actually done and the instructions given in connection with watered stock. In that inquiry as to watered stock, apart from the general instructions and general policy, how much further will you get, unless you go into particulars to see whether that policy has been lived up to or not, and how are you going to get those particulars, unless again this government breaks faith with its taxpayers? There is no secret whatever in the situation as to watered stock. Everybody who takes the trouble to look at the act knows it and it is no secret whatever.
I really would like to see something definite done one way or the other. Is the government content to waive the provisions of the act which in the last general election were alleged by hon. gentlemen supporting the Liberal party to have been specially arranged 20&i
so that one, Drayton, could get behind them? That is not only what was said but what certain newspapers printed. I should like to have something definite on this. I should like to know whether faith is to be kept or not, and if it is not, I want a hand in that inquiry. I can assure my hon. friends that it will be a bigger one than is here proposed; that I shall have not one answer but many more than one for everything that was said in connection with Riordou. How absurd the whole of this tissue of calumny was! Just for a few months did I know anything about the Riordon matter. My hon. friends have been in office and they have known all about it for two and one-half years. What have they done? Absolutely nothing. Pulp was away down; in the United States, our great market for the product of the Riordons' business was very bad in 1921, particularly bad in the summer of 1921. The market was off. Since then we have seen wonderful activity. We have seen that market taking all the pulp, yes, all the paper that can be offered. We have seen the price advance, yes, multiply. We have seen properties sold at far higher prices than they could have been sold at in those days. But nothing has been done. Why, some hon. gentlemen opposite thought that there should be a royal commission to investigate the Riordon charges. Yes, I was to be the subject of a royal commission. I have mentioned it before. I have invited it. I am getting tired of giving the invitation, but the invitation still stands. I should like an opportunity of meeting some of those valiant gentlemen before a royal commission where an oath could be taken and where it would amount to something. I should like something definite about this matter. Why, the last statement to the Riordon creditors-that is no secret now-shows that not a single soumarquee had been collected, nothing done by these hon. gentlemen that were so virtuous, so insistent and so indignant at a few months' delay. Yet nothing is done for two and a half years. I wonder if we can get something really straight and concrete, because I should like to have it.
As I said before, putting up with what I have put up with, I still say that, as a matter of public honesty, the act ought to be observed; but if that course is to be taken let it be taken openly, firmly, honestly. Do not let us have any more shilly-shallying about this. Either say we can go into this matter or not, what is the use of passing this resolution in view of the declaration already made on the one hand that details cannot be given, and, on the other hand, that details can be given. Why' should this House not know that? I want to know it and I want to be

Do I understand from the Prime Minister that this parliament has no right to order an investigation into methods of taxation or into any matter whatever affecting the welfare of this country? The Prime Minister quotes certain provisions of the act. As I understand that act, the provisions bind officials of the department to secrecy with regard to such information as comes before them. But I can hardly understand that the Prime Minister means that that act prohibits this parliament from making inquiries. I thought that this parliament could give instructions to any committee and that that committee could call before it what witnesses it would and ask from them what questions it would. Surely we are not going to abdicate all the rights of this House and say that we have erected all sorts of councils, commissions and departments which are out of our control? Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways):	I happened to be in the House
when this legislation was being discussed and I urged very strongly, as did others, that there should be an income tax, believing that this was a good way of finding money where money existed. But I did agree and am still of the opinion that any provision that would allow the examination into the private business of any firm or individual would not only be bad legislation but that it would wreck the results of the income tax law; because men can devise means of hiding their business transactions if they know that those transactions are to become public. This policy would be a fruitful field for the blackmailers and for all kinds of busybodies who perhaps might have no great interest in income tax themselves but who would fuss a good deal about the income tax of other people not being paid. It would make the conduct of business impossible so far as it related to the income tax.
I am strongly of the opinion that the income tax law is a just law. Theoretically we can talk on a good many subjects with more or less lucidity; but we have to be practical business men particularly in considering legislation which has to do only with business men. There is therefore no sense-and I do not say this offensively-in our endeavouring to find some means by which we can circumvent one of the protections that are afforded to those who are doing business, and so disclose the full particulars of people's affairs. One can imagine very many cases in which mischief might be done. I may refer to the Canadian National Railways, to which reference was also made by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth). The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) made out the whole case for the railways; he thought that it would be very detrimental to any company or individual if they were compelled to hand their private business over to the tender mercies of a rival for dissection.
As to the government's taking the ground that they must not say even who was at a cabinet meeting, the government did not take
any such ground. Those handling the case took the ground that they must not answer that question; for my part I answered, before the objection was taken, that I did not remember who was present; nor did I and members of the government who have attended cabinet meetings know that, except for some particular business between themselves, they never remember forty-eight hours after just who were present at any meeting. Their own business they will remember, and they will recall those who took part in the discussion; but apart from that their recollection will not be very precise. That, however, is merely by the way.
Let me point out that this parliament has a constitutional method of enacting legislation and of placing its views upon the statute books; and that is what the statute books are for. Parliament cannot one day pass an act, making the whole country liable tc it, and the next day through a committee violate that act. That could not be done. What would be the good of a statute if a committee could say, "We do not care anything for the statute; parliament has appointed us a committee to do certain things and we will do them irrespective of that law"? The king himself could not violate a statute without being brought to task, and this parliament has no right to break its own laws, it has no right to do so, either as a matter of law-if lawyers will allow me to say so-or as a matter of fair play and justice to the taxpayers who have sent them here. If this information is required ty parliament the right procedure is to repeal the statute and then let the committee fire ahead. But I am not in favour of this information being given, because I believe the business of the country at the present time is more sensitive than it has ever been before. If we repeal this statute we shall do more to injure business than all the one-horse investigations which may be carried on will do to help it.
What I am about to say is perhaps a little afield, but I am constrained to make this observation. The whole iworld just now seems to have a mania for investigating everybody but itself. Men in every parliament almost at the present time are on the lookout to see if they can find cause for investigating the other fellow for the purpose of getting something on him, as the saying is.

I think the statute is directed to preventing an individual employee from giving information in the course of his employment, and that means to any member of the public. I very much doubt if the statute at all prevents the exhibition of this information to the high court or parliament itself, but I prefer to put my ground for voting against this resolution on a very different plane. The mover has left this proposal, apparently purposely, in an absolutely nebulous, chaotic state; he has asked for parliament to send it to a committee without any additional facts and without any specific direction, and he has expressed to the House his entire willingness to have any change made that anyone else will offer which will make his motion wider. The hon. gentleman had control of the drafting of his amendment, and he could have made it wide enough to get at the specific thing which he desires to get at. I object to any more time being taken up in discussing some general principles or some theoretical possibilities in connection with our legislation. We have had altogether too much of that, and too little of the practical. We can sit in some committee for hours and discuss the whole scheme of the Income Tax Act and the Business Profits Tax Act over again. But are we going to get any further? Has anyone got a specific change to suggest? Does anyone say that the principle of income taxation is unfair? You will know nothing more when you get through an investigation of that character than you know to-day by intelligently reading the act. But we are not given the alternative, we are not given the form the*hon. mover suggested the investigation might take-that of specific inquiry. Therefore it is fair to conclude that this is simply one of the usual sandstorms that is blown up to attract public attention to some gentleman who poses as a great saviour of the unfortunate downtrodden people. He takes mighty good care not to put any punch into his proposition so anybody can possibly be hurt. To him the glory and to nobody any suffering. I am not going to vote for an investigation of that kind.

it make?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet."

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: This vessel was first called the "J. D. Hazen."

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What happened to her afterwards?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: She was sold to the Russian government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Did they give her the name "Mikula?"

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That was the name given to her by the Russian government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What has the Mikula cost since we re-purchased her?

They might call her the
"Alexander Johnston."

speechtext:
What are the
dates for the active campaign in ice-breaking?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

The requests begin about
the middle of January, and the work lasts up to the middle of April.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What is the ship used
for at this time of the year? Is she in commission?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, she is laid up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What is about the annual
cost of operation for that short season?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The cost is $192,800.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What crew does she carry
when in commission, and how much of a crew while she is not in commission? That is a large sum of money for the maintenance of a ship for a period of less than four months in the year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
She carries a crew of 84
men when in commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How many when she is laid
up?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When she is laid up the
crew consists of from 15 to 20 men.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What have 15 to 20 men
to do on a ship when she is laid up?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We have to take care of
the boat. It is necessary to have watchmen on the boat, and we have to keep her ready to render salvage service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What character of work?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
She is fitted for salvage
work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does she keep steam up
the year round?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: There was no call for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: How does the minister justify retaining 15 to 20 men on a ship that is laid up, and under no request for any kind of useful service? Is it true the department keeps on the whole staff-captain, first mate, second mate, third mate, first engineer, second engineer and third engineer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: We keep only two officers, the engineer and some men to perform necessary work on the ship. We also have the watchmen.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do you keep the cook on the boat?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, for these men.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: And the midshipmite?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How many ships has the
department in use, what are the names and where are they located?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The ships under this item
are 28 in number. Of these ships 20 are used on the Atlantic coast and the St. Lawrence, four on the inland waters, and four on the Pacific coast.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What are the names of
the ships on the inland waters?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Concretia at Prescott, the Grenville at Parry Sound, the Murray Stewart at Parry Sound, and the Scout al Prescott.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the Murray Stewart the vessel bought from Mr. J. F. M. Stewart, an alleged shipping man of Toronto, who has some relation with the Home Bank?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is she used for?

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
