maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is a very important vote for life saving service on both coasts and on the Great Lakes, but the provision is inadequate. I should like to find out on what principle the money is expended. Part of the vote relates to the maintenance of certain stations on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and on the Great Lakes, but the expenditure in the last case seems to be very small. I may say that formerly a life saving station was maintained in the port of Toronto, but four years ago the municipality was notified, through the Harbour Board1, that it would have to establish and maintain its own station. Consequently the Harbour Commissioners had to spend $60,000 to take care of the three million odd people that go in and out of the harbour of Toronto. And yet for the whole of the service comprised in this vote only $100,000 is asked. Part of this vote is to provide rewards for life saving at sea. That is all very well, but why not try and provide

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
also to a greater degree for the services which are rendered by the Harbour Commissioners of Toronto? Not only do they look after their own port but last summer they had to undertake work all over the Georgian bay and the Muskoka lakes; also at Hamilton, Oakville, Port Dalhousie, and points along the north shore of lake Ontario. Virtually they are maintaining a life saving station for lake Ontario, a thing which they have no power to do under their charter. Actually their work should be confined to looking after the millions of passengers who go from Toronto to Niagara, Hamilton, and other points. Take the north shore of lake Ontario and you will not find a single life saving station with the exception of the one at Toronto.
It is true the government gives a few hundred dollars to maintain a life boat at two or three small places, but what would happen in the case of an accident if the life boat was not up-to-date especially when it is remembered that it might take several hours to reach the scene. I call the minister's attention to the need of proper facilities in the Muskoka and Georgian bay districts which are visited annually by thousands of tourists. Last summer a serious accident occurred in the Georgian bay district. Three young men from my constituency were on their way up the Moon river when they unfortunately lost their lives. No life saving station nearer than Toronto was available for rendering assistance. Two or three life guards and some other help were sent up from Toronto, and the waters in the district were dragged for over a month without finding the bodies. I claim that the first duty of the department is to try and save the lives of the citizens of this country.
Complaints on this score are not confined to Toronto; they come from other places.The year before last there was an accident at Port Dalhousie. A poor girl was out on a raft, or some other contrivance, but there was no life saving station there to render her help, the nearest being at Toronto. The same situation exists at Grimsby beach and Burlington beach. I am sorry the member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) is not here to-night. I am sure that if he were he would support the plea I am making. There has been an insistent demand from the people of that city for a life saving station, also from the people of Oakville, and many places on the north shore of lake Ontario, east of Toronto. I suppose there are altogether two or three million people that go out from Toronto to Niagara, and other places, during the summer months. What would happen to a boat like the Cayuga, that carries several
hundred people, if she met with a mishap? And she did run on a sand shoal last summer. What would happen to the passengers of other boats running to Port Dalhousie, and other places, in the event of a mishap? Last summer a deck hand fell off a steamer running between Toronto and Rochester, and the body was not recovered for several months. The life saving appliance on the ship could not be lowered, and they did not even throw the poor deck hand a life belt. It is a very serious situation and I contend something ought to be done to provide an adequate remedy. The department abandoned the former system and told the people of Toronto some four years ago. "We will give you a few hundred dollars yearly but you will have to maintain your own station."
That the station is doing good1 work is shown by the fact that the last year it saved forty-four people from drowning. Had i". not been for the Toronto station that number of people would have lost their lives. I urge .the government to grant a larger vote for this purpose. The country is growing and the Canadians are an aquatic race. The possibility of accidents is increasing all the time. The loss of life at the summer resorts of Canada has been very large in comparison with our population. A great many of these deaths could have been prevented if we had had proper life saving stations and appliances in the districts to which I have referred. I would ask the minister now to grant a larger vote for this purpose. I would ask him also to consider the case of the relatives of the three young men who were drowned on the Moon river. The parents of these poor victims had to spend, I think, $2,000 in efforts to try and recover the bodies. Are we going to wait until a catastrophe occurs before voting increased sums for life saving purposes. The city of Toronto-which is overburdened with taxation, which is paying a very large sum annually to the government of Canada-[DOT] should receive some relief. The life saving work which was formerly carried on by the government there should be again taken over by them and the $60,000 which the city spends on life saving service, or a part of it, should be refunded to Toronto. Because, as I say, the life saving station at Toronto not only renders service on lake Ontario but also on the Muskoka lakes and the Georgian bay. The city of Toronto has been put to great expense in that regard, and has not been reimbursed for the large expenditure which it has incurred.

speechtext:
When danger arises at these different places on lake Ontario, they have had to wire the life saving station at Toronto to come and help to save lives. Lake Ontario is a very large area of water with a great deal of navigation. The number of steamboats on lake Ontario is probably larger than the number of boats on any of . the upper lakes. They do more actual passenger business, and the life-saving stations on lake Ontario are very inadequate. Is the department going to wait until they have a disaster in the Niagara district, Port Dalhousie or some other place on the lake before taking action? When will the department establish up-to-date life-saving stations on lake Ontario? At Charlotte and other places on the American side of lake Ontario they have proper life-saving stations. At Buffalo, at Toledo and at Detroit they have large up-to-date life-saving stations, these are under the control of the War department, and they are maintained by companies of men. At Buffalo they have a regular company of naval men who look after that particular port and there is a large volume of steamboat business there. Along the Great Lakes on the American side' [Mr. Hanson.J
they have proper life-saving stations. But what have we on the Canadian side of the border? We have one or two rowboats, or what they call lifeboats. We have small stations with very few boats. I maintain that we should have proper stations established on the Canadian side of lake Ontario if we are to make proper provision for the saving of lives. We have a station at Toronto which saved forty-four lives in four years, as a result of having up-to-date equipment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is cut out altogether up
west.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: The service has been about cut in two at Wood island. If hon. members will turn up the Auditor General's report they will see it cost nearly $14,000. I would like to know what the minister is doing as a matter of policy in connection with this matter; because I am sorry to admit that the Bay of Fundy is a very dangerous piece of water to navigate. In the parish of Grand Manan and on the southern portion of Nova Scotia, there have been a good many wrecks, and it is necessary to maintain at Grand Manan an up-to-date life saving station with all modem appliances. There have been a great many lives lost there in my own memory. Happily we do not have many wrecks, but when we do have a wreck it is a bad one and many lives are lost. As a resident of the country for many years and knowing perfectly the conditions that prevail there, I believe that station should be maintained in a thoroughly efficient manner. I should like to know the view of the department with regard to their policy at that particular station. The minister has made pretty good progress tonight, and if he will take a hint from his friends over here, he will let the committee rise and report progress.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will be quite ready to
accede to the suggestion of my hon. friend if he will let this item pass.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There seems to be a
feeling that an equitable policy is not being pursued with respect to life-saving stations; that certain sections are being allowed to save their own lives and other sections are being helped by the government. I do not think the passing of this act will ever save the government's life. The minister has put through ten items tonight, involving something like two million dollars, and this has been done since half past ten. We cannot be sitting here till midnight continuously.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
As Bill No. 47, incorporating the United Church of Canada, stands in my name, and, I hope, will be reached to-morrow evening at eight pm., I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if he, with the consent of the House, would agree to set 'apart Wednesday, June 18, for consideration of this bill, if not disposed of on Tuesday evening. Its importance not only to the millions of people directly interested, but to the country as a whole, I submit, places the bill in the same position as a public bill. With the consent of the Prime Minister, I would move, seconded by Mr. Putnam:
That Bill No. 47, incorporating the United Church of Canada, be the first order for Wednesday, June 18, and given precedence until disposed of unless disposed of on Tuesday evening.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before that motion is put, it seems to me that it is rather unusual. Members who are interested in this bill should have been consulted with regard to the matter. I have made an important engagement in Montreal for Wednesday, and I should like to be present when this bill is reached. I, therefore, object to this motion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: It has to be unanimous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There Wias no intention of
causing any inconvenience to anyone. During the last few days there has been general talk around the House that this bill was coming up on Wednesday, and this was only for the purpose of facilitating business. If any inconvenience is going to be caused to anyone who wishes to take part in the debate, I understand the consent must be unanimous. No discourtesy was meant in making the motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The government rather
hoped that it might be possible to dispose of the bill to-morrow evening in the regular order. Certainly, if it is not disposed of then, it would be our wish to expedite the disposition of it. On the other hand, it requires the unanimous consent of the House to change
Mr. Murdock and Home Bank

the order. If it can be arranged to the satisfaction of members of the House to have the bill proceeded with on Wednesday, assuming that it cannot be disposed of to-morrow night, the government will be only too ready to acquiesce in the request of my hon. friend, but he understands, of course, that it is open to any hon. member to object.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-TAX COLLECTIONS PROPOSED INQUIRY BY PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As this motion requires the unanimous consent of the House, it would require to stand until Wednesday when the order is called, when that consent may be given.
Motion stands.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.45 u.m.
Tuesday, June 17, 1924
